HEADLINE: Streamer scrambles to fix faults
TEXT:
Optus has suffered a nightmare start to its high-profile push into mainstream sports broadcasting, with thousands of fans left fuming over the weekend as its FIFA World Cup coverage buckled under the weight of numbers.

The country's second largest telecommunications company has invested a huge amount of money and credibility on a plan to become recognised as a soccer broadcaster, and the beginning of the World Cup in Russia this weekend was its big moment to prove it could deliver.

The telco has the lion's share of rights to the world's biggest sporting event, with traditional broadcaster SBS showing one match a day - leaving Optus to exclusively broadcast many of the tournament's biggest matches via its Optus Sport online streaming service.

However, as fans gathered for World Cup parties around the country and others settled in at home to watch Egypt vs Uruguay (with an expected duel between Premier League star Mohammed Salah and Barcelona ace Luis Suarez), many were left disappointed on all counts. Optus cannot be blamed for Salah spending the whole match on the subs bench but it is in the crosshairs for the failure of its systems to handle viewer demand.

In echoes of its early days as the exclusive broadcaster of the English Premier League back in 2016, thousands of fans were left trying to troubleshoot dodgy live streams instead of enjoying the football.

Many of these viewers have paid $15 a month to sign up for the service during the World Cup, and calls for refunds were deafening.

While some viewers had no problems with the coverage on both the Fetch TV app and the smartphone app, the number of angry customers taking to social media in impotent rage about buffering or constantly crashing streams, indicates that Optus has messed up its big moment badly.

Amid its Tweets and Facebook posts attempting to gee up enthusiasm for the ongoing games, the Optus Sport social media team belatedly recognised that nobody wanted to talk to them about Luis Suarez missing a chance and admitted that they were being besieged by complaints.

"We apologise that some viewers are experiencing technical difficulties. If that is you - go to sport.optus.com.au to watch Morocco v Iran live." It posted, sending viewers to a web browser rather than their mobile or TV apps.

However, it didn't take long for people to report that this link was crashing as well. Thankfully for all concerned, the Socceroos' match against France (like all their games) was simulcast on free-to-air SBS.

Later on Saturday night, some users, although fewer than the previous night, again reported issues watching Lionel Messi's Argentina take on fan-favourites Iceland. On Sunday, Optus played down the extent of the problem and appeared to give assurances the issue was under control.

"We have seen a large demand for our streaming service and the overwhelming majority of people have had a positive experience," an Optus spokesman said. "Unfortunately, a small number of customers who watched the match on the Optus Sport app, on certain devices, experienced some buffering issues."

While its statement plays down the extent of the problems, and there will have been plenty of viewers who enjoyed the coverage, the technical problems are the absolute last thing that soccer-mad Optus chief executive Allen Lew will have wanted.

The company has been preparing for the tournament for months and should not have been taken by surprise.

For what it's worth the content of Optus' coverage has been excellent so far and it would be a real shame for everyone if it spoiled it all with technical inadequacy.

Here's hoping for a better performance from here.

HEADLINE: State Street used Fearless Girl to face bull and drive change
TEXT:
When getting the Fearless Girl campaign ready for launch, the State Street Global Advisors marketing team was prepared for the worst.

The global fund manager, along with its advertising agency McCann, installed a bronze statue of a defiant girl standing head on with Wall Street's famous Charging Bull in the New York's financial district to shine a light on its push for more women in boardrooms and the promoting of its gender diversity exchange-traded fund, which allows investors to invest in companies with higher levels of gender diversity in leadership positions.

State Street's marketing and communications team was prepared for backlash because they knew they were inviting scrutiny of themselves.

"We feel comfortable that the issue of gender diversity within our own company is an area where we are very committed," State Street Global Advisors vice-president of marketing communications and global marketing Liz Serotte, who was part of the team who created the Fearless Girl campaign, told The Australian Financial Review. "We've made steady progress and we can point to a lot of the advances that we've made in the past five years or so in hiring women at executive levels, promotions of women at executive levels. But we're not flawless. We certainly never intended this to be a celebration of our own accomplishments and did not intend to hold ourselves up as the poster child for this and indicate that anyone should model themselves on us."

The reaction was overwhelmingly positive. The Fearless Girl campaign went global quickly after its launch on International Women's Day in March 2017. In the 12 weeks after it launched, the campaign garnered 4.6 billion Twitter impressions, 745 million Instagram impressions, was mentioned in 1676 broadcast TV segments and was in 2400 news articles.

"It was huge, we were getting things like the game show Jeopardy," Ms Serotte said.

"A movie that wanted to shoot a scene, a women's health and fitness magazine wanted to do a photo shoot with the star of a hit TV show and all these things you just don't anticipate."

The company wasn't just marketing a message - it truly believed it and used its influence as a global fund manager to drive change.

Across Australia, the United States and United Kingdom, State Street contacted 700 companies and voted against 500 of them with no women on their boards at annual general meetings.

Of those 500, 152 have added a female board member and 34 are committed to doing so. In 2018, State Street is continuing to pursue the strategy of voting for more women on boards and is expanding its scope into Japan and Canada.

In the first few days after the unveiling of Fearless Girl, State Street saw a 170 per cent increase in inflows to its products. But Ms Serotte said the campaign was more focused on creating awareness of State Street's investment philosophy to "invest responsibly to enable economic prosperity and social progress".

The Fearless Girl statue, which took on a meaning of its own well beyond State Street's intentions, initially had a permit to be in place for seven days. Now, more than a year on, it still stands as part of New York City's public arts program and will be moved to stand outside the New York Stock Exchange this year. "While this is a statue that inspired many, [it] has taken on many different meanings for many different people, which we are delighted to see," Ms Serotte said. "We've been very disciplined about not latching on to all these different messages or things that others have associated with the statue and stayed to this core message around the power of women in leadership that I think is ultimately what made the campaign so successful for us and so impactful."

HEADLINE: Optus takes aim at more Euro football
TEXT:
Optus is running the ruler over bids for more European football competitions, including Germany's Bundesliga, Spain's La Liga and Italy's Serie A.

The Singtel-owned telecommunications provider has been steadily building its football offering, starting with the English Premier League, which it re-signed for another three years, as revealed by The Australian Financial Review in April.

The telco is broadcasting every game of the World Cup from Russia, which began last week, finishing the long-tail contract for the 2020 European Championship and is believed to be the frontrunner to secure rights to the Champions League, up against incumbent beIN Sports Australia.

It comes as Optus was hit with a rough start to its World Cup coverage on Friday night with many experiencing issues with a live stream between Egypt and Uruguay. Optus apologised for the issues and worked over the weekend to minimise problems.

Sources said Optus is looking to sweep up a number of European domestic competitions, including Germany, Spain, Italy and France, which on their own don't draw huge audiences in Australia, but if secured, help the telco build out its strategy of being the home of international football.

Optus is known to be in the market for additional content to reinforce the telco as the home of elite football. The telco declined to comment of what specific competitions it was looking to add.

The EPL and World Cup are the most popular football competitions in the world, both of which Optus has secured, so any additional leagues would be complementary rather than be a standalone drawcard.

These rights have largely been held by Qatari-owned beIN Sports Australia. The sports channel, the previous holder of the Euros, looks like missing out on the Champions League, and was the under-bidder when Optus first sprung on the EPL in 2015.

beIN Sports had hoped to set up a EPL Asia-Pacific hub, but missing out on Australia in 2015 to Optus - it also looks likely to lose the rights in New Zealand and Indonesia - has dashed the Al-Jazeera-owned sports broadcaster. Industry insiders have begun to question what beIN Sports' approach to the Australian market will be moving forward.

Football has been a key point of differentiation for Optus under chief executive Allen Lew, since he took up the job in 2014. Optus swooped in on EPL rights in 2015 with a $63 million a year bid for the competition, beating out incumbent rights holder Fox Sports.

The second season of Optus' EPL coverage has just ended, and combined with a deal it struck with National Geographic in July 2017, it has helped the telco grow its customer base.

Over the 12 months to March 31, Optus had its strongest year of postpaid mobile subscriber growth since its 2010-11 financial year, adding 357,000 new customers in the segment.

Content is becoming an increasingly important differentiator for telcos who are facing poor margins on the national broadband network and declining average revenue per user. Telcos are betting on quality content offers making customers stickier.

Telstra signed a deal for mobile rights to the A-League, W-League, non-World Cup Socceroos and Matildas matches in May, to go with its digital rights to the NRL, AFL and netball.

Football has been a key point of differentiation for Optus under chief executive Allen Lew.

HEADLINE: Nine, ANC to launch business journalism JV
TEXT:
Nine Entertainment and Australian News Channel are launching a new business, personal finance and lifestyle journalism joint venture, including a new free-to-air and pay television channel, Your Money, which will replace Sky News Business.

The 50-50 joint venture, foreshadowed by The Australian Financial Review in March, will seek to capitalise on the rise of the number of self-managed super funds and growing interest in business beyond specialist corporate coverage.

Nine chief executive Hugh Marks told the Financial Review the venture will cater to "the needs of people in this world where they're needing to understand what their life has got in store for them and how they get there".

He said Your Money, which will be broadcast on free-to-air and subscription television, and other digital properties in the venture would be a different take on business news, one more oriented to a broader consumer group and will include areas such as financial services, real estate, travel, luxury and consumer goods.

"If you look at our business and think about what's happening to media, our ability to build a business solely based on selling 30-second ads both has it's challenges going forward ... but there are also opportunities because you can reaches audiences in many different ways," Mr Marks said. "You now to start to add on to that relationship you have with an advertiser."

Mr Marks said while the new 24/7 channel was a key pillar of the venture, it was a digital-first initiative and would provide a new marketing platform for advertisers to be more integrated.

"You've got to change your whole philosophy about how a relationship looks into the future," he said.

The new offering will also allow Sky News Business, which will cease airing when the venture launches, to get its content to a wider audience beyond Foxtel, which is in just under 30 per cent of Australian homes.

"We are setting the stage for a bold new era in business and finance news and commentary in Australia - with a new go-to channel for viewers, businesses and advertisers," said ANC chief executive Angelos Frangopoulos.

"Our joint venture will take our business and finance content to even wider audiences, bringing together leading business journalists and commentators on the country's foremost business and personal finance channel."

Nine and ANC, which is owned by News Corporation, will base the new Your Money channel out of the Rupert Murdoch-controlled company's Holt Street Australian headquarters. Kylie Merritt, who is currently ANC commercial director, will be chief executive of the new venture, and David Ash, formerly of Nine digital, will be head of digital for the new business.

ANC has been searching for ways to take its content beyond subscription television. In May, it signed a deal with regional broadcaster WIN Corporation for a new 24/7 news channel, Sky News on WIN, across 29 regional markets.

News Corp bought ANC from Nine, Seven and Britain's Sky in 2016 for around $25 million. It has been keen to get Sky News content on free-to-air TV after its plans to do so on Network Ten were nixed when it was bought by CBS last year.

News Corp co-chairman Lachlan Murdoch and WIN owner Bruce Gordon launched a joint bid for Ten, which would have seen Sky News content integrated with the free-to-air broadcaster's news offering. However, it was not to be.

We are setting the stage for a bold new era in business and finance news. Angelos Frangopoulos, ANC

HEADLINE: Deals come to a head on out-of-home advertising
TEXT:
The consolidation of Australia's out-of-home advertising sector is ramping up as French giant JCDecaux's move for APN Outdoor could come to a head and oOh!media swooped on Adshel for $570 million at the weekend.

JCDecaux and APN Outdoor started engaging overnight on Friday, as revealed by The Australian Financial Review on Saturday morning.

It is understood APN Outdoor's management presented to the board of JCDecaux in the early hours of Saturday and both parties, along with their advisors, were working late into Sunday night to try to get a deal done.

The time zone difference between Sydney and Paris has made negotiations during the daytime in Australia difficult. Australia could wake up on Monday to an accepted takeover bid from JCDecaux for APN Outdoor, the two parties could be continuing negotiations, or either party could walk away.

JCDecaux is advised by Goldman Sachs, while APN Outdoor has Cadence Advisory in its corner.

JCDecaux offered $1.1 billion for APN Outdoor on Wednesday evening, but the Australian company's shareholders said the price was too low at $6.52 per share, an 11 per cent premium to Wednesday's close price of $5.85.

Paris-based JCDecaux has a strong balance sheet and should be able to fund an acquisition quite easily from attractive European debt markets.

It comes as APN Outdoor lost out to rival oOh!media for Here, There & Everywhere's Adshel, as first reported by the Financial Review on Saturday.

oOh!media offered $570 million in cash versus APN Outdoor's $540 million mix of cash and shares.

It is understood oOh!media will launch an equity raising, comprised of a $320 million rights issue, to fund the purchase on Monday.

Credit Suisse and CLSA advised HT&E, while Highbury Partnership and Macquarie tended to oOh!media.

HT&E shareholders are believed to be happy with the $570 million price tag, which is $150 million above oOh!media's first approach in April and $100 million above its second approach in May. APN Outdoor entered the fray with a $500 million approach before increasing it at the bid deadline on Friday.

In 2016, HT&E, then known as APN News & Media, paid $268 million for the 50 per cent of Adshel it didn't already own, valuing the business at $536 million.

It came under fire from shareholders who questioned whether the company paid too much after it lost the valuable Yarra Trams contract in 2017.

It's understood the HT&E board is focused on capital management, with debt reduction, a special dividend and share buyback all being considered.

APN Outdoor put forward a $540 million final bid for Adshel, comprised of $230 million in cash and a further $310 million in scrip, or 54.1 million shares, for HT&E's existing shareholders.

APN Outdoor was initially planning an all-cash offer which would have been funded by a $250 million to $300 million capital raising. However, the approach from JCDecaux forced it to take another route.

HEADLINE: Trump's media critics need him but food might be a comfort
TEXT:
Could food save journalism after Trump is gone?

At The Washington Post this month, a group of media executives from around the world was greeted by a shining food laboratory.

The Post is known for its political coverage. It has invested in writing about food too. A recipe database on the paper's website can be searched by ingredients, a regular columnist, Dorie Greenspan, has written a dozen cookbooks, and there are at least nine other reporters and editors who cover food, cooking, wine and restaurants. Regular food videos are shot inhouse. The latest is on camel milk, which is good for lactose-intolerant people.

The Post and The New York Times have experienced a surge in readership from their Trump coverage. Not only are readers around the world fascinated by the unconventional President, the two papers have reached deep inside the White House to reveal the inner workings of presidential politics.

One example of compelling reporting: Trump and Malcolm Turnbull's telephone bust-up over a deal to transfer refugees agreed by the Obama administration. The Post still has a transcript of the prematurely terminated call online.

Other news outlets are having success covering the beat too, including start-up Axios, where Australian journalist Jonathan Swan is building a reputation as a news breaker.

At the World Congress of News Media conference in Washington this month, media executives around the world heard that the Trump news bump had bifurcated the US newspaper industry into haves and have-nots. The presidency is great for the Post and the Times, which are reporting a welcome uptick amid a long decline in the news business. At the Post, website visitors rose 3.5 per cent to 84 million in May from a year earlier, giving it the third-biggest digital audience after CNN and the Times.

But the rest of the industry is losing readers, ad revenue and good journalists, to the industry leaders.

The Times and the Post are enjoying success now, but if the Republican president isn't re-elected in 2020, they are going to be back facing the same problems undermining their rivals. Paradoxically, the papers that are doing the most to expose the problems of the Trump presidency may have the most to lose if he does.

Right now, the most worrying business problem looks like an acceleration in the decline of digital advertising revenue.

Despite early hopes, display ads - ads with graphical or photographic images - haven't taken off on newspaper websites. Google and Facebook are sucking up a lot of what might have been that ad revenue, undermining newspapers and journalism vital to democracy and civic society.

To their credit, both tech companies are aware of their pernicious impact, and are working with publishers to help them make more money from journalism. They want to be seen as friendly. At the Washington conference, Google hosted drinks for the newspaper executives at the famous Hay-Adams Hotel near the White House.

The digital ad decline - call it the second stage of the digital transformation - is driving papers into the arms of their online readers. The Australian Financial Review has always charged for access to its website. Rivals such as The Australian are now concentrating more on online access too.

In marketing circles it used to be called building subs. Today the terminology is generating membership. By providing extra services, including special deals and events, "members" are less likely to cancel their newspaper subscriptions, marketing executives believe.

Papers are also going back to an old-fashioned business tactic: move sidewards. Some papers are finding puzzles and food can be just as important as breaking news. Sometimes they combine both. One of the many articles in Washington Post during last week's diplomatic meeting in Singapore was titled: "The culinary diplomacy of the Trump-Kim summit lunch menu."

The two papers have reached deep inside the White House.

HEADLINE: New tax threatens to cost Amazon $4.5b
TEXT:
Behind Amazon's decision to place a geoblock on its Australian customers last week is that the US online giant is facing the threat of new taxes that could cost it more than $4.5 billion.

The real impact of Amazon's Australian move is the message it sends to the European Commission and US states that it will resist attempts to impose new turnover taxes and it is prepared to punish governments that pursue them. The stakes are way beyond any problem with paying Australia's newly legislated 10 per cent GST on online sales.

The US Supreme Court is expected to hand down its ruling late this month on South Dakota v Wayfair Inc, a decision that will recast the future of online retailing, one way or the other.

The court decision could potentially cost Amazon more than $3.5 billion, just as the European Commission's call for a 3 per cent digital tax on online turnover could cost Amazon another $1 billion.

It's in this context that Amazon last week announced that it was too onerous to calculate the 10 per cent GST due on sales to Australia from its US and European operations and therefore will stop all shipments to Australia from July 1, forcing Australians to buy from its smaller local arm.

"While we regret any inconvenience this may cause customers, we have had to assess the workability of the legislation as a global business with multiple international sites," Amazon said.

How did it get to this?

The history of US online retailing has been shaped by the 1992 case Quill v North Dakota, where the US Supreme Court found that a state could not levy sales tax on an online purchase - in this case, Quill was selling software programs on floppy disks - if the vendor had no physical presence in the state.

Most US states depend upon sales taxes of between 6 per cent and 9 per cent for a major part of their income. So the Quill ruling automatically gave online sellers a 6 to 9 per cent price advantage over conventional retailers.

South Dakota says that US states miss out on $US33 billion in sales tax on online sales because of Quill. Congress's Government Accountability Office puts the figure between $US8.5 and $US13.4 billion.

The retailer which has benefited most from this is Amazon. Its retail arm is a low-margin business, which reported $US106 billion of US sales last year. By next year Amazon is expected to account for just over half of all US online sales.

But in recent years its business model has changed to emphasise Amazon Prime's distribution outlets, which gives it a physical presence in each state. So it has begun paying sales tax.

But that only applies to Amazon's own products. Almost half of what it sells involves third-party vendors, which it says have no physical presence in other states so pay no sales tax. That would be something like $US50 billion of sales with no tax.

So Amazon has most to lose if the Supreme Court overturns Quill in the South Dakota v Wayfair Inc case - and some believe the court would not have accepted the case if the justices were not considering doing just this.

HEADLINE: Disruptors increase traditional TV spending
TEXT:
Despite being cast as a long-term disruptive threat to the viability of commercial television networks, new figures show tech giants Google, Amazon, Uber and Apple have significantly increased the amount they spend on traditional television advertising in Australia.

Figures sourced from Nielsen Adex by TV industry group ThinkTV showed Google had the biggest percentage increase in TV spend in the e-commerce category, raising its outlay by 600 per cent to $11.3 million as it launched new products such as Google Home and Google Pixel.

Apple, meanwhile, increased its TV spend in Australia 17.4 per cent to $20.2 million in 2017, as the world's most valuable company sought to promote launches including the iPhone X, and a new mobile-enabled Apple Watch.

Online retail colossus Amazon also backed its Australian launch with its first ever local TV ad campaign, spending $3.2 million, while ridesharing firm Uber also started advertising on Australian TV with $3.4 million.

The managing director of independent marketing and media consultancy Ebiquity Asia-Pacific, Richard Basil-Jones, said while the spending in traditional media channels by tech disruptors could be seen as counter-intuitive, it showed recognition that TV still offered an ability to reach an important group of consumers.

"There's no one medium that fits the bill and all media recognise the strengths of other media," he said. "The biggest e-commerce and online players recognise what TV offers and TV is open and smart enough to understand that they need to embrace online too."

Google Australia and New Zealand director of marketing Aisling Finch said its increased TV ad spending was part of its plans to use a range of advertising channels.

She said Google recognised that audiences engage with content across different platforms at different times.

"For campaigns such as the launch of Google Home we used a combination of radio, TV, cinema, print, outdoor and online channels including search, YouTube and social," Ms Finch said. "In this campaign we found the combination of contextual media and creative drove stronger uplift."

ThinkTV, which sourced the statistics, is a research and marketing body for commercial broadcasters, owned by Foxtel, Nine Entertainment, Seven West Media and Ten Network, and as such is partly focused on demonstrating the value of TV advertising.

Its chief executive, Kim Portrate, said she was delighted to see some of the world's fast-growing, most innovative companies investing more into TV advertising to grow their brands. She said companies were also increasingly using TV ads in partnership with online-only content.

"The smartest brands know that TV reaches more people faster than any other media, is brand safe, generates the greatest return on investment and commands the most attention, which translates directly into sales," Ms Portrate said.

In February ThinkTV revealed KPMG figures had shown the metropolitan free-to-air TV market returned to growth for the first time in 3½ years, growing by 1.4 per cent to $1.5 billion in the six months to December.
